stances.claim: Many readers asked why Filipino lawyers are fond of citing the American Supreme Court and American jurists -- the short answer is that PH political, constitutional, international, corporate, and tax laws are American in origin; US precedents are cited as authority for local litigations involving the same facts and issues as American counterpart cases

Jurisprudence is authoritarian in the sense that sometimes logic is not enough to understand and interpret a legal provision; it should be buttressed by accepted usages and precedents from the foreign jurisdiction where the legal provision was sourced

In the not-so-distant past, our SC also relied heavily on Spanish decisions and authorities like Manresa and Sanchez Roman in interpreting civil laws (family, marriage, property, inheritance, basic commerce) because our Civil Code and old Code of Commerce were sourced from Spain -- same source-jurisdiction principle

On the June 18, 2002 visit to the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa hosted by CJ Beverley McLachlin, Sr. J. Claire L'Heureux-Dubé broke the ice by observing that PH decisions liberally quote Holmes, Hugo Black, and Felix Frankfurter but have yet to cite the Canadian SC -- to which CJP parried: 'I must admit that Your Honor is correct... But may I also venture my respectful observation that I, too, have yet to read a Canadian decision citing the Philippine Supreme Court'

CJP took the banter to heart -- after returning to the Philippines, he penned People v. Genosa (January 15, 2004) adopting for the first time the 'battered woman syndrome' as a form of self-defense, or at least a mitigating circumstance, in a parricide prosecution committed by a wife against her husband; he expressly cited a Supreme Court of Canada decision as authority and sent a copy to the Ottawa justices

The encounter may have been minor in the great history of the Canadian Court but was a major event of CJP's judicial career -- CJ even remembers the menu (onion soup, gingered steak with Napa cabbage salad, vanilla ice cream with fresh fruits, coffee/tea); it is not every day the Canadian SC goes out of its somber ways to host and banter with jurists from a little country halfway across the globe

CJP used the opportunity to invite McLachlin to visit PH, which she did in October 2006 -- attended the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (CJP's valedictory as CJ); 300+ CJs/jurists/lawyers attended; she so loved it here that she extended her stay from three days to one week; Ateneo conferred an honorary law doctorate; gamely danced the swing and the boogie with CJP at the farewell party

Incidentally, the Asean chief justices at the invitation of CJ Sereno will be in PH late February for the ALA General Assembly in Makati and Boracay -- the official host is the ALA Philippines Chapter headed by Accra Law's top honcho Avelino V. Cruz (foreshadowing E95, B06, B17)

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a recurring reader question: why are Filipino lawyers so fond of citing the American Supreme Court and American jurists to support their cases and causes? His short answer: because PH political, constitutional, international, corporate, and tax laws are American in origin. US precedents in these subjects are cited as authority for local litigations involving the same facts and issues as American counterpart cases. Jurisprudence is authoritarian in the sense that sometimes logic is not enough to understand and interpret a legal provision -- it should be buttressed by accepted usages and precedents from the foreign jurisdiction where the legal provision was sourced. In the not-so-distant past, the PH SC also relied heavily on Spanish decisions and authorities like Manresa and Sanchez Roman in interpreting civil laws (family affairs, marriage, property relations, inheritance, basic commerce) because the Civil Code and the old Code of Commerce were sourced from Spain. This same question of why PH lawyers lean heavily on American authorities was asked when CJP and some SC colleagues visited the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa. The Chief Justice of Canada, the Right Honorable Beverley McLachlin, hosted lunch in the inner sanctum of the Canadian Court (known simply as the 'Judges' Dining Room') on Tuesday, June 18, 2002. After breaking bread, they were ushered to an internal conference room for a lively discussion. To start the dialogue, Senior Justice (now retired) Claire L'Heureux-Dubé remarked: 'I notice that your decisions in the Philippines liberally quote from the US Supreme Court, especially from Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Hugo Black and Felix Frankfurter. However, I have yet to see one that cites our Supreme Court or our Canadian justices.' For a moment the delegation was stunned into speechlessness; but after a second or two of silence, CJP found his tongue and replied: 'I must admit that Your Honor is correct. In its over 100 years of history, our Supreme Court has not used a Canadian precedent to buttress its judgments. But may I also venture my respectful observation that I, too, have yet to read a Canadian decision citing the Philippine Supreme Court.' That exchange of banter broke the proverbial ice, leading to more in-depth discussions on the role of the judiciary in respective nations' history and development. CJP took the banter to heart. After returning to the Philippines, he penned People v. Genosa (January 15, 2004) adopting for the first time the 'battered woman syndrome' as a form of self-defense, or at least a mitigating circumstance, in a parricide prosecution committed by a wife against her husband. In that landmark case, he expressly cited a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada as authority -- and made sure a copy was sent to the justices in Ottawa. The encounter may have been a minor incident in the great history of the Canadian Court, but it was a major event of CJP's judicial career. He even remembers the menu: onion soup, gingered steak with Napa cabbage salad, vanilla ice cream with fresh fruits, and coffee/tea. It is not every day that the Canadian Supreme Court goes out of its somber ways to host and banter with jurists from a little country halfway across the globe. CJP used the opportunity to invite McLachlin to visit PH, which she did in October 2006 -- attending the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity, which CJP convened as his valedictory as chief justice. Over 300 chief justices, jurists, and lawyers from all over the world attended, but the brilliant Canadian CJ so loved it here that she extended her stay from her original three days to one week. McLachlin is the first woman and longest-serving chief justice in Canadian history. She started her term on January 2, 2000 and will end it on September 7, 2018 when she turns 75 -- the retirement age in her country (it is 70 here). Ateneo de Manila conferred on her, during her extended stay, an honorary doctoral degree in law. Though appearing stoic and unreachable while presiding on the bench, she is cordial and friendly in informal gatherings among colleagues. She could eloquently deliver scholarly speeches just as she could gracefully pirouette on the stage; she gamely danced the swing and the boogie with CJP during the farewell party. CJP and wife Leni cherish a personal friendship with her and her low-profile husband Frank who accompanied her. At another time, CJP will relate his encounters with other foreign counterparts -- especially the Spanish, Chinese, Russian, Egyptian, and Asean judiciaries -- and will also recall an interesting conversation with then Spanish Prime Minister Jose Zapatero during a luncheon hosted in Madrid. Incidentally, the Asean chief justices, at the invitation of CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, will be in the Philippines in late February to attend the General Assembly of the Asean Law Association in Makati and Boracay (foreshadowing E95, B06, and B17). The official host is the ALA Philippines Chapter headed by Accra Law's top honcho, Avelino V. Cruz.
